prose_changes.old: In 1312 the Council of Vienne's decree Ad nostrum listed eight errors said to belong to beguines and beghards in Germany. Their core claim was that a soul made perfect in this life needs neither the church nor the virtues any longer. Interrogators then went looking for people who held them. They found them, because the questions supplied the answers. Robert Lerner's 1972 study concluded that no organized sect of this kind ever existed. What existed was a wide spectrum of mystical piety, much of it among beguines and beghards, and a charge that could be laid against any part of it. Marguerite Porete's own book, once separated from the label, has since been read as a serious work of theology.

prose_changes.old: In the early fourteenth century the church declared that a sect existed. The decree Ad nostrum, issued at the Council of Vienne in 1312, listed eight errors said to be held by beguines and beghards in Germany. Their core claim was that a soul made perfect in this life can no longer sin, and needs neither the church nor the virtues any longer. One error spoke of people living 'in the spirit of liberty'. Interrogators then went looking for people who held them, and found them, because the questions supplied the answers. Modern research, above all Robert Lerner's study of 1972, concluded that no organized sect of this kind ever existed. What existed was a wide spectrum of mystical piety, much of it among beguines and beghards, and a charge that could be laid against any part of it. The movement named here probably was not real; the charge and its victims certainly were.

prose_changes.old: Across a single century, a scattering of English men and women began writing about the inner life of prayer. They wrote in their own language rather than in Latin. Richard Rolle, the Yorkshire hermit, wrote the Fire of Love. Walter Hilton wrote the Scale of Perfection. An author whose name is lost wrote The Cloud of Unknowing. All of them wrote for recluses and devout lay people rather than for scholars. Two of the voices are women's. Julian of Norwich was an anchoress, enclosed in a cell beside a Norwich parish church. She spent decades revising an account of sixteen revelations she had received during a near-fatal illness. In the end she reached the line she is still known for: that all shall be well. Margery Kempe was a brewer's wife from Bishop's Lynn who could not write. Her own book says she bore fourteen children. She dictated to scribes a book about her pilgrimages, her uncontrollable public weeping and the heresy examinations she survived. It is the closest thing the period leaves us to an ordinary believer's own life story. Carthusian monks copied The Cloud and Hilton's Scale and kept them safe.

All of them wrote for recluses and devout lay people rather than for scholars. Two of the voices are women's. Julian of Norwich was an anchoress, enclosed in a cell beside a Norwich parish church. Margery Kempe, a mayor's daughter from Bishop's Lynn, ran a brewery of her own for a few years. She could not write. Her own book says she bore fourteen children. prose_changes.old: The Viking wars nearly killed English Christianity, by Alfred of Wessex's account. He wrote that the churches had been ravaged and burned. Whole dioceses lapsed. When Alfred set out to rebuild, he complained that he could hardly find a priest south of the Thames able to translate a Latin letter. His answer was a program of translation. Gregory the Great's Pastoral Care and other books the clergy needed were put into English, so that they could read them at all. And the Chronicle begun in his reign is the first sustained history written in English. A century later came a second rebuilding, led by the bishops Dunstan, Æthelwold and Oswald. They refounded the monasteries on the Rule of Benedict and drew up one agreed customary for the whole country. The English language stayed central throughout. Ælfric wrote sermons in English, well over a hundred by his editors' count, so that ordinary people could hear careful teaching in their own tongue. Archbishop Wulfstan preached in 1014 as the Danish invasions closed in. He told the English that their own sins had brought the calamity on them. The Norman Conquest of 1066 ended the church's independent growth.

prose_changes.old: Byzantine heresy hunters say the Paulicians rejected the Old Testament, the cross and the sacraments. Whether they truly believed that, or their enemies needed them to, cannot now be settled. No account of their faith in their own words survives. What is certain is what happened to them. Imperial armies killed them and drove them from their homes. The survivors built a fortified state at Tephrike on the frontier. By Byzantine accounts they raided the empire's lands until it fell in 878.

By Byzantine accounts they raided the empire's lands until the town fell in 878.

prose_changes.old: The Paulicians appear in the record from the seventh to the ninth century, in Armenia and eastern Anatolia. Almost everything said about them was written by people trying to destroy them. Byzantine heresy-hunters say the movement rejected the Old Testament, the cross, the sacraments and the honor paid to Mary. They say it held that the world was split between a good power and an evil one. Whether they truly believed that, or their enemies needed them to, cannot now be settled. What is not in doubt is what was done to them. Imperial armies killed and uprooted them in large numbers. The survivors built a fortified state of their own at Tephrike on the frontier, and made common cause with the Arabs. By Byzantine accounts they raided the empire's lands until the fortress fell in 878. Later emperors forced whole Paulician groups to move to the Balkans.

prose_changes.old: The Rule became the standard for monks in the West. Carolingian reformers made it the norm across the Frankish empire. It stands behind the Cluniacs, the Cistercians and the Benedictine congregations that keep it today. Its language of stability, obedience and moderation reached far beyond the cloister. So did the way it built the day around fixed hours of prayer, and both passed into the West's habits of work and time. Monte Cassino itself was destroyed again and again, and rebuilt every time. Paul the Deacon tells how the Lombards sacked it. Later records add the Saracens, an earthquake, and Allied bombing in 1944. Monks live there now.
prose_changes.new: The Rule became the standard for monks in the West. Carolingian reformers made it the norm across the Frankish empire. It stands behind the Cluniacs, the Cistercians and the Benedictine congregations that keep it today. Its language of stability, obedience and moderation reached far beyond the cloister. So did the way it built the day around fixed hours of prayer, and both passed into the West's habits of work and time. Monte Cassino itself was destroyed again and again, and rebuilt every time. Paul the Deacon tells how the Lombards sacked it. The abbey's own medieval chronicle tells of a Saracen attack. An earthquake later brought it down, and in 1944 Allied bombing destroyed it. Monks live there now.
prose_changes.reason: R1-09: the Saracen attack names its witness (the Chronicle of Monte Cassino, wanted). The earthquake is not violence; the 1944 bombing is an admitted, recorded act (see for_mark).

prose_changes.old: In 1270 the Solomonic dynasty took the Ethiopian throne, and a wave of monks came with it. Tekle Haymanot and the followers of Ewostatewos led them, and they carried churches deep into newly won lands. The Ewostathians kept Saturday as well as Sunday as a Sabbath. The lives of their own saints say they were persecuted for it for generations, until the emperor Zara Yaqob gave way at a council in 1450. His court chronicle says he ordered the old Sabbath kept as holy as Sunday. The same emperor wrote books of theology. He persecuted the monks of Estifanos when they refused to bow before Mary and the cross. It was all written down in Ge'ez: royal chronicles, saints' lives, hymns to Mary, and the Kebra Nagast. That book gave the dynasty its claim to come down from Solomon and Sheba.
